concept: Form I assimilated (mithāl) verb وَعَدَ — jussive/imperative deletes the first radical wāw, so the imperative needs no prosthetic hamza
prompt: Give the masculine-singular direct imperative of وَعَدَ (Form I, imperfect يَعِدُ), and state whether it needs an opening prosthetic hamza.
expected_answer: عِدْ — the imperative needs no prosthetic hamza, because deleting the first-radical wāw leaves the stem opening directly on the voweled consonant ع, and a prosthetic hamza is only added to support a stem that would otherwise open on a vowelless consonant.
accepted_variants: عِدْ with no prosthetic hamza: after the first-radical wāw is deleted, the stem already opens on a voweled consonant, so there is nothing for a hamza to support.
forbidden_answers: إِعِدْ — a prosthetic hamza opens the imperative, exactly as a sound verb's imperative needs one.
أَوْعِدْ — the imperative keeps the first radical wāw.
required_reasoning: first-radical wāw deleted in the jussive/imperative stem
the resulting opening consonant already carries its own vowel so no prosthetic hamza is licensed
explanation: A prosthetic hamza is added only to a jussive/imperative stem that would otherwise open on a vowelless consonant, as in ordinary sound verbs (اُكْتُبْ). An assimilated verb's jussive/imperative already deletes the first radical wāw, so the stem opens directly on a voweled consonant (عِدْ) and needs no such support.

concept: Form I assimilated verb وَصَلَ — the first radical wāw is deleted from the Form I imperfect stem, not merged onto the middle radical while retained
prompt: Give the Form I imperfect (huwa, indicative) of وَصَلَ, and state what happens to the first radical wāw.
expected_answer: يَصِلُ — the first-radical wāw is deleted from the Form I imperfect stem entirely; the tense prefix attaches directly to the second radical ص, not to a retained wāw.
accepted_variants: يَصِلُ, with the first-radical wāw deleted from the imperfect stem entirely, not merged or retained.
forbidden_answers: يَوْصِلُ — the first radical wāw is carried into the Form I imperfect stem.
يَاصِلُ — the first radical wāw shifts to a long alif instead of deleting.
required_reasoning: Form I imperfect stem of an assimilated verb
first-radical wāw deleted, not retained or merged
explanation: The Form I imperfect stem of an assimilated verb has no slot at all for the first radical: the tense prefix attaches directly to the second radical, so يَصِلُ is the whole word, never يَوْصِلُ with the wāw carried into the imperfect.

concept: Form IV أَوْصَلَ (root و-ص-ل) keeps its first radical wāw in the imperfect; the Form I deletion rule does not extend to derived forms
prompt: Give the Form IV imperfect (huwa) of the root و-ص-ل (أَوْصَلَ, 'to deliver/connect'), and state whether the first radical wāw is deleted.
expected_answer: يُوصِلُ — the first radical wāw is kept; Form I's imperfect deletion rule is scoped to the Form I imperfect vowel pattern only and does not extend to Form IV or any other derived form.
accepted_variants: يُوصِلُ, keeping the wāw, since the deletion rule belongs to Form I only and derived forms never delete it.
forbidden_answers: يُصِلُ — the first radical wāw is deleted from the Form IV imperfect exactly as in Form I.
يُوَصِّلُ — Form II's template is used in place of Form IV.
required_reasoning: Form IV imperfect stem
first-radical wāw retained because deletion is a Form I fact only, never extended to derived forms
explanation: First-radical wāw-deletion is conditioned on the Form I imperfect vowel pattern; Form IV's own template does not share that condition, so its imperfect keeps the wāw as an ordinary consonant: يُوصِلُ, never the Form-I-style يُصِلُ.

concept: a retained first radical after a derived-form prefix (يُوعِدُ, Form IV of وعد) is not evidence the verb is still Form I
prompt: يُوعِدُ is the Form IV imperfect of وَعَدَ. A learner reads the retained و after the prefix and concludes the verb must still be Form I, since Form I's وعد usually deletes that wāw. Correct this and name the verb's actual form.
expected_answer: يُوعِدُ is Form IV (أَوْعَدَ), not Form I; the retained wāw after the prefix is exactly what Form IV's own template predicts, since Form I's deletion rule does not apply here — the form is fixed from the prefix vowel and template shape, not from whether a radical is retained.
accepted_variants: The verb is Form IV, أَوْعَدَ, because the form is fixed from the prefix vowel and template shape; a retained radical after a derived-form prefix does not mean the verb reverted to Form I.
forbidden_answers: it must be Form I because the wāw should have deleted, so يُوعِدُ is an irregularly retained Form I imperfect.
يُوعِدُ is a Form I imperfect with the wāw kept as an exception.
required_reasoning: the form is fixed from the prefix vowel and template shape, not from whether a radical is retained
the retained wāw is exactly what Form IV's own template predicts, not evidence of Form I
explanation: The form of a verb is fixed by its prefix vowel and stem template before any gloss is assigned. يُوعِدُ carries the Form IV prefix vowel and template, so its retained first radical is exactly what that derived-form template predicts — it is never grounds for reclassifying the verb as Form I.

concept: defective verb imperfect subtype vowel is stored per verb: دَعَا -> يَدْعُو (u-type) vs رَمَى -> يَرْمِي (i-type) are not interchangeable
prompt: Give the Form I imperfect (huwa) of دَعَا ('to call, invoke') and of رَمَى ('to throw'), and state whether their subtype vowels are interchangeable.
expected_answer: يَدْعُو (u-type) and يَرْمِي (i-type) — the two subtype vowels are not interchangeable; each defective verb's subtype is a stored lexical fact, so writing يَدْعِي for دَعَا or يَرْمُو for رَمَى produces a shape neither verb actually has.
accepted_variants: يَدْعُو and يَرْمِي, two different stored subtype vowels that cannot be swapped between these verbs.
forbidden_answers: يَدْعِي and يَرْمُو — the subtype vowels are swapped between the two defective verbs.
both verbs share one imperfect subtype vowel because both are defective.
required_reasoning: each defective verb's imperfect subtype vowel is a stored lexical fact
the two subtype vowels are not interchangeable between verbs
explanation: Defective Form I verbs split into different lexically stored imperfect subtypes (e.g. the u-type يَدْعُو and the i-type يَرْمِي); the subtype is a per-verb fact, not a free choice, so exchanging the two subtype vowels between دَعَا and رَمَى yields a form neither verb actually has.

concept: defective verb masculine plural past — the consonant-initial وا suffix forces the final weak radical to shift/reappear rather than keeping the bare past's long vowel (the same rule also governs a doubly-weak/lafīf verb's plural past)
prompt: Give the masculine plural past (hum) of رَمَى ('he threw'), and state what happens to the final radical before the plural suffix.
expected_answer: رَمَوْا — the consonant-initial وا suffix forces the underlying weak final radical back as a glide (و) before the suffix; the bare past's long alif (رَمَى) is not available in this suffixed cell.
accepted_variants: رَمَوْا, since the plural suffix triggers the final-radical shift that the bare past's long vowel does not show.
forbidden_answers: رَمَىوا — the bare past's long alif is kept directly before the plural suffix.
رَمُوا — the shift produces a different (wāw-final) verb's plural shape.
required_reasoning: a consonant-initial plural suffix triggers the final-radical shift
the bare past's long vowel is not available once a consonant-initial suffix follows
explanation: The bare past رَمَى shows its weak final radical only as a long vowel; a consonant-initial suffix such as the masculine plural وا forces that underlying radical to shift back to a glide, giving رَمَوْا — never the ungrammatical stacking of the bare long vowel directly against the suffix. The identical shift governs a lafīf (doubly weak) verb's own masculine plural past.

concept: defective verb jussive deletes the final weak radical outright, rather than keeping it under a sukūn as a sound verb's jussive would
prompt: Give the jussive (majzūm) huwa form of يَرْمِي after لَمْ, and state what happens to the final radical.
expected_answer: لَمْ يَرْمِ — the jussive deletes the final weak radical ي outright; it is not kept and marked with sukūn the way a sound verb's final consonant would be.
accepted_variants: لَمْ يَرْمِ, with the final ي deleted outright rather than kept under a sukūn.
forbidden_answers: لَمْ يَرْمِيْ — the final radical ي is kept and marked with a sukūn under the jussive.
لَمْ يَرْمِي — the jussive leaves the indicative ending unchanged.
required_reasoning: jussive operator لَمْ present
final weak radical deleted outright, not marked with sukūn
explanation: A sound verb's jussive adds sukūn to an intact final consonant; a defective verb's jussive instead deletes the final weak radical entirely, so لَمْ يَرْمِ ends on the second radical, with no trace of the ي and no sukūn to place on it.

concept: a suffixed past cell selects the underlying consonant radical, never the bare past's long alif
prompt: Give the past tense of رَمَى with the first-person-singular suffix تُ (أنا), and state whether the bare past's long alif survives before this suffix.
expected_answer: رَمَيْتُ — the consonant-initial suffix تُ forces the underlying weak radical back as ي; the bare past's long alif (as in رَمَى) is only available in the unsuffixed cell and never appears before a consonant-initial suffix.
accepted_variants: رَمَيْتُ, since a consonant-initial suffix always selects the underlying radical, never the bare past's long alif.
forbidden_answers: رَمَىتُ — the bare past's long alif is kept directly before the suffix.
رَمَتُ — the final radical is dropped rather than restored before the suffix.
required_reasoning: a consonant-initial suffix selects the underlying radical
the bare past's long alif is not available once a suffix is attached
explanation: The long alif of رَمَى is the bare (unsuffixed) past's own realization of the final weak radical; the moment a consonant-initial suffix such as تُ attaches, that same radical must resurface as its underlying consonant (ي), giving رَمَيْتُ, never a suffix stacked directly onto the long alif.

concept: geminate verb imperfect vowel is a stored per-verb fact: مَدَّ -> يَمُدُّ (u) vs فَرَّ -> يَفِرُّ (i) are not predictable from the geminate class alone
prompt: Give the Form I imperfect (huwa) of مَدَّ ('to extend') and فَرَّ ('to flee'), and state whether their middle imperfect vowels are predictable from the geminate class alone.
expected_answer: يَمُدُّ (u-type) and يَفِرُّ (i-type) — the middle imperfect vowel is not predictable from the geminate class alone; it is stored with each verb's own lexical entry, exactly as with sound verbs.
accepted_variants: يَمُدُّ and يَفِرُّ, two different stored vowels; the geminate class does not fix one uniform vowel for every member.
forbidden_answers: both verbs take the same imperfect vowel because they are both geminate verbs.
يَمِدُّ and يَفُرُّ — the imperfect vowels are swapped between the two verbs.
required_reasoning: the middle imperfect vowel is stored per verb
geminate class membership alone does not fix that vowel for every member
explanation: Like ordinary Form I sound verbs, a geminate verb's own middle imperfect vowel is a lexical fact stored with that verb, not a consequence of belonging to the geminate class; مَدَّ and فَرَّ show that two geminate verbs can take two different vowels.

concept: the shadda on a geminate verb realizes two identical root consonants; it is never dropped as if merely decorative
prompt: Give the Form I imperfect (huwa) of مَدَّ, and state what the shadda on the doubled consonant represents.
expected_answer: يَمُدُّ — the shadda represents two identical root consonants merged together (the second and third radicals, both د); dropping it would remove one of the verb's three radicals from the word entirely.
accepted_variants: يَمُدُّ, whose shadda stands for two root consonants merged together, not an optional decoration.
forbidden_answers: يَمُدْ — the shadda can be dropped since it is only a stylistic pronunciation detail.
the shadda on a geminate verb is optional stylistic gemination.
required_reasoning: the shadda realizes two identical root radicals merged together
dropping the shadda removes a radical from the word
explanation: A geminate root has two identical consonants in its second and third radical slots; when nothing blocks their merger, they surface as one consonant carrying a shadda. That mark is a radical count, not a stylistic flourish, so it is never optional.

concept: a consonant-initial suffix forces separation of a geminate verb's two identical radicals, blocking merger
prompt: Give the past tense of مَدَّ with the first-person-singular suffix تُ (أنا), and state whether the two identical radicals stay merged before this suffix.
expected_answer: مَدَدْتُ — the consonant-initial suffix تُ forces the two identical radicals apart (separation), because merging them would stack a doubled consonant directly against another vowelless consonant, which the language disallows.
accepted_variants: مَدَدْتُ, with the radicals separated because a consonant-initial suffix blocks their merger.
forbidden_answers: مَدَّتُ — the two radicals stay merged directly before the consonant-initial suffix.
مَدَتُ — one of the two identical radicals is simply dropped before the suffix.
required_reasoning: a consonant-initial suffix follows
merger is blocked and the radicals separate rather than staying merged or being dropped
explanation: Gemination (merger) is licensed only where nothing vowelless immediately follows the doubled consonant. The first-person-singular past suffix تُ opens with a consonant, so the two identical radicals must separate: مَدَدْتُ, never a merged shadda stacked against another consonant.

concept: geminate verb مَدَّ — merger is obligatory once a vowel immediately follows the second radical (e.g. the masculine-plural indicative suffix), so separating the radicals in that cell is ungrammatical; this obligatory-merger cell is distinct from the jussive/imperative cell, where nothing follows and BOTH merger and separation are licensed (see WRV-13)
prompt: Give the Form I imperfect indicative (hum, masculine plural) of مَدَّ, and state whether the two identical radicals may separate in this suffixed cell.
expected_answer: يَمُدُّونَ — the radicals merge here obligatorily, because the plural suffix's own vowel immediately follows the second radical; a following vowel never licenses separation, unlike the jussive/imperative cell where nothing follows and either shape is licensed.
accepted_variants: يَمُدُّونَ, with the radicals obligatorily merged because a vowel immediately follows the second radical in this suffixed cell.
forbidden_answers: يَمْدُدُونَ — the radicals are separated even though a vowel immediately follows the second radical, which makes merger obligatory here.
يَمْدُدُونَ — separation is licensed here just as it is in the jussive cell, since both are cells of the same geminate verb.
required_reasoning: a vowel immediately follows the second radical in this suffixed cell
merger is obligatory whenever a vowel immediately follows the second radical
the separated shape licensed in the jussive/imperative cell does not carry over to this vowel-following cell
explanation: Merger and separation of a geminate verb's two identical radicals are conditioned by what follows the second radical, not by the verb's identity: a vowel immediately following (as in the plural-indicative suffix, هُمْ يَمُدُّونَ) makes merger obligatory, exactly as in the plain indicative يَمُدُّ. The jussive/imperative cell's own two licensed shapes (merged-with-fatḥa or separated-with-sukūn, see WRV-13) belong to a DIFFERENT environment, where nothing but sukūn/pause follows the second radical; that licensed separation never transfers to a cell where a vowel follows.

concept: the geminate jussive after لَمْ has two SECURELY licensed shapes, merged-with-fatḥa or separated-with-sukūn — this pair is not asserted as the complete classical inventory of licensed shapes; a merged form with ḍamma is simply the indicative, not a jussive shape at all
prompt: A learner writes لَمْ يَمُدُّ (merged, with ḍamma) as the jussive of مَدَّ after لَمْ. Correct this and give a licensed jussive shape.
expected_answer: لَمْ يَمُدَّ (merged with fatḥa) or لَمْ يَمْدُدْ (separated with sukūn) are two securely licensed jussive shapes; لَمْ يَمُدُّ keeps the indicative's ḍamma and is not a jussive shape at all. This pair is taught as securely licensed EXAMPLES, not as a claim that they exhaust the classical geminate-jussive inventory.
accepted_variants: the jussive لَمْ يَمُدَّ or لَمْ يَمْدُدْ are two securely licensed shapes, not the ḍamma-marked لَمْ يَمُدُّ, which is simply the indicative; this does not claim to exhaust every licensed geminate-jussive shape.
forbidden_answers: لَمْ يَمُدُّ is a valid jussive shape merged with ḍamma.
the jussive of a geminate verb always keeps the indicative's ending unchanged.
required_reasoning: merged-with-fatḥa and separated-with-sukūn are two securely licensed shapes for the geminate jussive
a merged form carrying ḍamma is the indicative, not a jussive option
explanation: A geminate verb's jussive is securely realized as the merged shape with fatḥa on the doubled consonant, or as the separated shape with sukūn on the first of the two radicals; a merged shape carrying ḍamma is not a jussive option at all — it is simply the indicative, unaffected by the jussive operator. This row teaches only that these two shapes ARE licensed; it does not assert they are the only ones, and it neither accepts nor hard-rejects a further merged-vowel (kasra/ḍamma-by-itbāʿ) variant independent review has raised — closing that question needs dedicated scholar review outside this bounded repair.

concept: hamza carrier chosen by comparing the hamza's own vowel with the vowel before it: سَأَلَ (alif carrier) vs سُئِلَ (yāʾ carrier) show the same root taking different carriers
prompt: Give the Form I active past (سَأَلَ) and the Form I passive past (سُئِلَ) of the root س-أ-ل ('to ask'), and justify why the hamza's carrier differs between the two.
expected_answer: سَأَلَ (alif carrier) and سُئِلَ (yāʾ carrier, dotless ئ) — in the active past the hamza's own vowel (fatḥa) and the vowel before it (fatḥa) both point to alif; in the passive past the hamza's own vowel (kasra) outranks the vowel before it (ḍamma), so the carrier switches to yāʾ.
accepted_variants: سَأَلَ with alif and سُئِلَ with yāʾ (ئ); the vowel on the hamza and the vowel before it decide the carrier, and that decision changes between the active and passive past.
forbidden_answers: سُأِلَ — the alif carrier from the active past is kept in the passive past.
سَئَلَ — the yāʾ carrier from the passive past is used in the active past.
required_reasoning: the carrier is decided by comparing the hamza's own vowel with the vowel immediately before it
the active and passive past have different vowel environments, so they take different carriers
explanation: A hamza's carrier is never fixed to the root; it is chosen by comparing the vowel written on the hamza itself with the vowel on the letter immediately before it, and picking the carrier that matches the stronger of the two. The active and passive past of the same root, سَأَلَ and سُئِلَ, show two different carriers precisely because their vowel environments differ.

concept: أَخَذَ، أَكَلَ، أَمَرَ have a small, stored, closed list of irregular hamza-less imperatives: خُذْ، كُلْ، مُرْ
prompt: Give the masculine-singular imperative of أَخَذَ ('to take'), and state whether it follows the regular hamza-carrier rule.
expected_answer: خُذْ — this is one of a small, lexically stored set of three initial-hamza verbs (أَخَذَ، أَكَلَ، أَمَرَ) whose imperative is formed WITHOUT the hamza at all; it is not derived from the regular carrier rule and must be checked as a stored exception.
accepted_variants: خُذْ, one of the three stored hamza-less imperatives (with أَكَلَ giving كُلْ and أَمَرَ giving مُرْ), not a regular carrier-rule output.
forbidden_answers: أُخُذْ — the regular root hamza is kept in the imperative.
اِخُذْ — a prosthetic hamza replaces the root hamza in the imperative.
required_reasoning: one of a small stored list of three verbs with an irregular, hamza-less imperative
the form is not produced by the regular carrier rule and must be checked as a lexical fact
explanation: أَخَذَ، أَكَلَ، and أَمَرَ are the three Form I hamzated verbs whose imperatives drop the root's own initial hamza entirely: خُذْ، كُلْ، مُرْ. This is a small, closed, memorized list — not an application of the ordinary carrier rule — so no other initial-hamza verb's imperative may be predicted from it.

concept: رَأَى has a stored irregular Form I imperfect with no hamza at all: يَرَى, not a regularly-derived يَرْأَى
prompt: Give the Form I imperfect (huwa) of رَأَى ('to see'), and state whether it carries a hamza.
expected_answer: يَرَى — this member has a stored irregular imperfect with NO hamza at all; restoring a regular hamza (as in a hypothetical يَرْأَى) produces a non-word, because this verb's imperfect is a lexical exception, not a regular derivation.
accepted_variants: يَرَى, with no hamza; the regularly-derived يَرْأَى is not the attested form for this irregular member.
forbidden_answers: يَرْأَى — a regular hamza is restored into the imperfect of this irregular member.
يَرْءَى — the hamza is kept but moved to a different carrier.
required_reasoning: this verb's imperfect is a stored irregular lexical fact
restoring a regular hamza into this cell produces a non-existent form
explanation: Most hamzated verbs keep their hamza throughout the imperfect and only need its carrier re-checked; رَأَى is an exception stored as a lexical fact: its imperfect يَرَى has no hamza at all. Reconstructing a regular hamza-bearing form here does not recover a suppressed regularity — it produces a word that does not exist.

concept: a hamza radical is a separate class from the weak (wāw/yāʾ) radicals; weak-root rules such as hollow-verb contraction never transfer to it
prompt: A learner runs سَأَلَ's medial hamza through the hollow-verb (weak middle radical) contraction rule and expects a contracted imperfect like a hollow verb's. Correct this and give the actual Form I imperfect (huwa).
expected_answer: يَسْأَلُ — the middle radical of سأل is a hamza, not a weak wāw/yāʾ radical, so the hollow-verb contraction rule (which deletes or lengthens a weak middle radical) does not apply to it at all; the hamza surfaces as an ordinary, if carrier-marked, consonant in every cell.
accepted_variants: يَسْأَلُ, since the middle radical is a hamza, a separate class from the weak radicals, so no hollow-verb contraction applies.
forbidden_answers: يَسَالُ — the hollow-verb contraction rule is applied to the medial hamza.
يَسْلُ — the medial hamza is deleted as if it were a weak radical.
required_reasoning: a hamza radical is a separate class from the weak wāw/yāʾ radicals
weak-root rules such as hollow-verb contraction never apply to a hamza radical
explanation: Hollow-verb contraction is triggered specifically by a weak (wāw/yāʾ) middle radical; a hamza is phonologically and orthographically a distinct radical class, so even though it needs its own carrier rule, it never contracts or deletes the way a true weak radical does. سَأَلَ keeps a full three-consonant shape in every cell: يَسْأَلُ.

concept: hamza carrier re-evaluated after suffixation for a final-hamza verb: قرأ's singular-cell carrier (alif) is not simply copied into the plural cell; two spellings are BOTH licensed for the plural cell (bare hamza, or a wāw carrier), since a wāw-carrier hamza directly adjacent to the plural's own wāw is conventionally simplified to a bare hamza in some orthographic traditions but kept as a wāw carrier in others
prompt: Give the Form I imperfect huwa (يَقْرَأُ) and hum (masculine plural, 'they read') of قَرَأَ, and state whether the singular's alif carrier is kept in the plural.
expected_answer: يَقْرَأُ (huwa, alif carrier) and, for hum, either يَقْرَءُونَ (bare hamza) or يَقْرَؤُونَ (wāw carrier) — both are licensed spellings of the plural cell. The plural suffix changes the hamza's surrounding environment (its own ḍamma now outranks the preceding fatḥa, which licenses a wāw carrier), so the singular's alif carrier is not simply copied into the plural cell; some orthographic conventions simplify the wāw-carrier hamza to bare (on the line) immediately before the plural's own wāw to avoid writing wāw twice, while others keep the wāw carrier, so either is accepted — but copying the singular's alif carrier unchanged is never licensed.
accepted_variants: يَقْرَأُ with alif in the singular verb cell; for the plural, either the bare-hamza spelling يَقْرَءُونَ or the wāw-carrier spelling يَقْرَؤُونَ is licensed, since the carrier is re-checked (never copied) after the suffix, and both are accepted spellings of the resulting environment.
the plural cell licenses two spellings, يَقْرَءُونَ (bare hamza) and يَقْرَؤُونَ (wāw carrier); the singular's alif carrier from يَقْرَأُ is never simply copied into either.
forbidden_answers: يَقْرَأُونَ — the singular's alif carrier is copied unchanged into the plural cell.
يَقْرَاُونَ — a carrier is invented that the plural environment does not license.
required_reasoning: the hamza's carrier is re-evaluated after every affixation
the plural suffix changes the vowel environment of the verb cell, so the singular's alif carrier is not simply copied
both the bare-hamza and wāw-carrier plural spellings are licensed; only the copied singular alif carrier is forbidden
explanation: A hamza's carrier is decided from its immediate environment, and that environment changes the moment a suffix attaches to the verb cell. The singular's alif carrier in يَقْرَأُ reflects that cell's own environment only; once the masculine plural suffix is attached, the hamza's own ḍamma outranks the preceding fatḥa, licensing a wāw carrier (يَقْرَؤُونَ) — but because that carrier wāw would sit directly before the plural suffix's own wāw, some orthographic conventions simplify it to a bare hamza (يَقْرَءُونَ) instead; both spellings are attested and licensed. What is never licensed is copying the singular's own alif carrier unchanged into the plural cell.

concept: lafīf subtype fixed by radical position: وَفَى (weak C1+C3 = mafrūq) vs طَوَى (weak C2+C3 = maqrūn) have different imperfect shapes and lengths
prompt: Name the lafīf subtype of وَفَى and of طَوَى from the positions of their weak radicals, and give each verb's Form I imperfect (huwa).
expected_answer: وَفَى is mafrūq (separated: weak radicals at C1 and C3) with imperfect يَفِي; طَوَى is maqrūn (joined: weak radicals at C2 and C3) with imperfect يَطْوِي — the two subtypes are fixed by radical position and their imperfects differ in shape and length, never conflated into one pattern.
